description:
White Rock lake, Winfrey Point

description:
I was fairly amazed to see that Baltimore Orioles and Orchard Orioles seem to  tolerate each other without territorial squabbles - or at least I've not seen any evidence of disputes. 

This beautiful male Baltimore Oriole was happily singing in this tree that is on the site of the ruined foundations of a small barn about six meters above a tributary of Buffalo Creek. 

After I took the first of these photos I listened to Yellow Warblers, Common Yellowthroats, and American Redstarts singing, mostly just out of sight, for fifteen minutes, when I heard, saw, photographed, and recorded a male Orchard Oriole singing for a few minutes in this same tree! 

Just *five minutes* after the Orchard Oriole flew on, I took the second of these photos of the same (or another?) Baltimore Oriole back in the very same tree. They were just taking turns in this popular spot. Is that usual? Do these two species just get along really well? It's fantastic to see them both practically together in any case. 

Unfortunately, five days later, a male Baltimore Oriole was found dead on the road not far away. I can't quite imagine how that happens - a car killing a songbird on a fairly quiet rural road. Speeding? Sad.

I have been spending some time recently photographing and recording both Baltimore Orioles and Orchard Orioles on the farm , and have seen more this year than ever before,... 
[see: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/162015181
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/162010999] 
...so, it was especially  sad to see one killed on the road. I can’t quite imagine how that happens on a relatively quiet rural road such as ours. Even if the bird was eating bugs off he pavement, there would be plenty of time to slow down or stop. Collisions at the speed limit with birds flying across the road don’t seem very likely where visibility is good either. Puzzling. Oh well, we still have a living pair in our farmyard. 

I wonder how numerous they really are here? 
How could one know? 
No matter. They are amazing.

I had a little more time than a few days ago and found some species (magnolia warbler, Swainson's warbler, white-eyed vireo) in the same spots they were in last time, so I guess they are waiting for the stormy weather to pass before moving on. I did see bigger numbers overall than a few days ago but having more time meant I was able to check spots a little more thoroughly. Was hoping badly to pick up a couple more uncommon/rare warblers (blackburnian/bay-beasted/blue-winged/yellow/prothonotary/hooded/Nashville) to try to hit a magical 20 warblers but it just didn't happen.

I had a job in St. Petersburg beginning at 1900, so we left "early" so that I would not be late for work.
